tier_reason: ePrint 2025/377 Table 10 does compare HiAE against OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM on 14 named CPUs with GCC version and -O3 stated, but the paper is a non-peer-reviewed preprint by the designers (ePrint lists 'Publication info: Preprint'; no venue found on Crossref), and the public harness (test/performance_test.c) times only HiAE with no OpenSSL/baseline code, so it is neither A (baseline benchmark code not public) nor B (not peer-reviewed/independent).

corrections.claimed_speedup: AEAD at 16384 B (Table 10): 340.02 Gbps (HiAE) vs 51.90 Gbps (OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM) on AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (~6.6x, derived from page data); 171.46 vs 36.49 Gbps on Intel Xeon W9-3495X (~4.7x, derived from page data); 253.19 vs 38.80 Gbps on AMD EPYC 9334 (~6.5x, derived from page data). The abstract states over 340 Gbps on x86 and 180 Gbps on ARM in AEAD mode, 'making it the fastest AEAD solution on ARM chips and setting a new performance record on the latest x86 processors'.
corrections.hardware: 14 CPUs in Table 9/10: Intel Xeon W9-3495X, AMD EPYC 9334, AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, Intel Xeon Gold 6326, Intel Core i7-11700, Intel Xeon Gold 6242R, Intel Xeon E5-2620 v3, HiSilicon Kunpeng 920, Kunpeng 920X, Kirin 9000S, Qualcomm Snapdragon 8+ Gen1, Apple M2 Max, Apple M3 Pro, Rockchip RK3568 (an M1 MacBook Air is named in the setup text but has no result row)
corrections.caveats: Very new design (2025) by the paper's authors; numbers are first-party, from a non-peer-reviewed preprint. The public repo harness (test/performance_test.c) benchmarks HiAE only; the OpenSSL comparison code is not published. On mobile phones the AES-256 baseline was hand-implemented rather than OpenSSL. HiAE trails Rocca on pre-VAES Xeons (Gold 6242R, E5-2620 v3). Under active cryptanalysis: ePrint 2025/1180 'Cryptanalysis of the Authenticated Stream Cipher HiAE' (now a minor revision of a ToSC 2026 paper), 2025/1203 'Analyze the Security of the AEAD Scheme HiAE by Algebraic Techniques', and the designers' rebuttal 2025/1235. The reference repo has no license file; an MIT-licensed implementation exists at hiae-aead/libhiae (59 stars), but its README does not benchmark against AES-GCM.

notes: All three quoted numbers match Table 10 exactly; the only fix is marking the ratios as derived (7950X is 6.55x, not 6.5x). Metadata checked: no LICENSE file, not archived or a fork, 21 stars, last commit 2025-11-11 (active). Orchestrator may prefer hiae-aead/libhiae (MIT) as the copyable repo, but that is a different project URL, so I did not change repo_url.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed paper (ePrint 2018/1143, published by the IACR in FSE 2020). Table 3 shows SNOW-V-GCM beating OpenSSL 3.0.0-dev AES-256-GCM asm at 16 KB on a named i7-8650U. It falls short of A: compiler flags are only 'most possible optimizations switched on', the benchmark harness adapted from OpenSSL is not published, and the benchmarked AVX2/PCLMULQDQ SNOW-V-GCM build is not printed (Appendix D has a portable GHASH reference, and Appendix E has AVX2 code only for the SNOW-V keystream).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Table 3, AEAD, 16384 B: 38.91 Gbps (SNOW-V-GCM C++) vs 34.42 Gbps (OpenSSL AES-256-GCM asm), ~13% faster (derived from page data). Roughly even at 2048 B (30.71 vs 30.49); AES-256-GCM wins at 1024 B and below (e.g. 64 B: 8.54 vs 5.16 Gbps).
corrections.caveats: Single 2018-era ultrabook CPU against a pre-release OpenSSL snapshot (3.0.0-dev, 2019-04-01); the win is small (~13%) and only above ~2 KB. The paper prints the SNOW-V AVX2 keystream code and a portable SNOW-V-GCM reference, but not the PCLMULQDQ-optimized GCM build or the harness that produced Table 3. Counter-evidence: HiAE (ePrint 2025/377, Table 10) measured the official SNOW-V-GCM implementation well below OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM on every modern x86 CPU tested (e.g. 19.92 vs 51.90 Gbps on Ryzen 9 7950X, 13.04 vs 36.49 Gbps on Xeon W9-3495X at 16 KB). No maintained public repo, so usability is 'reference'.

notes: Numbers and setup (VS2017 + NASM, i7-8650U, single thread) match the paper exactly. The tier drops from A to B because neither the flags nor the benchmarked code/harness are public. Consider flagging this entry, because a later third-party measurement (the HiAE paper) contradicts the speed win on current CPUs.

tier_reason: ePrint 2026/1338 ('Bitslicing the AEGIS', Frank Denis) is a preprint by the repo author, not a peer-reviewed paper, so the evidence is first-party and B does not apply. It is not A either: the public harness (src/test/benchmark.zig) times only AEGIS, not the OpenSSL/BoringSSL AES-GCM baselines, and compiler/flags are unstated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper Table 2, 16 KB messages, vs side-channel-protected (bitsliced) AES-128-GCM: ARM Cortex-A53 423 Mb/s (AEGIS-128L) vs 261 Mb/s (OpenSSL 3.3), 1.6x; SpacemiT X60 RISC-V 193 (128L) / 333 (128X2) vs 137 Mb/s (BoringSSL), 1.4-2.4x; SiFive U74 182 / 311 vs 130 Mb/s, 1.4-2.4x; WebAssembly on an Apple M1 host 2241 / 2912 vs 480 Mb/s, 4.7-6.1x. Cortex-M4: 185 cycles/byte (bitsliced AEGIS-128L) vs 246 (fixsliced AES-128-GCM, protected GHASH) and 208 (unprotected table AES-128-GCM). Table 3, pure TypeScript on Apple M5 Max/Bun, 1 MB: 324 MB/s (AEGIS-128L) vs 182 MB/s (noble AES-128-GCM, 1.8x) and 256 MB/s (noble ChaCha20-Poly1305, 1.3x).
corrections.caveats: Published 2026-06/07 as a non-peer-reviewed preprint by the implementation's author; not yet independently reproduced. The C/Zig benchmark harness (src/test/benchmark.zig) measures only AEGIS variants; the baseline AES-GCM runs are not part of the published code, and compilers/flags are unstated. The repo README currently shows different, higher WebAssembly figures (AEGIS-128X2 3154, AEGIS-128L 3429 Mb/s) than the paper (2912 / 2241 Mb/s). The JS comparison uses the companion repo jedisct1/js-aegis-aead, whose 'bun run bench' does include noble-ciphers, but that baseline is not the listed OpenSSL/BoringSSL one.

notes: All claimed numbers appear in the paper, but the X60 figure (333 Mb/s) is AEGIS-128X2, not 128L, so I labeled the variants. GitHub reports license NOASSERTION; the LICENSE file is plain MIT (Frank Denis, based on Adomnicai's work). Repo: 9 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-21 (active). ePrint lists the paper as CC0, but the code is MIT.
